title: In the age of AI, the future needs humans. But for what?
excerpt: Your value grows when you can frame the problem, check the answer and take responsibility for the decision.
author: Anzolo Kpazhi Hope

paragraphs: You watch AI write a proposal in seconds. It summarises a report that would have taken you an hour. Then a question arrives that is more personal than technical: if the machine can do this, where do I fit?

I understand why that question matters. My answer begins with the part of the job that is easy to overlook: deciding what deserves to be done, what a good result means and whether the answer fits the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Your profession is a starting point
paragraphs: If you are a teacher, you know the difference between a correct answer and a student who understands. If you manage sales, you know that a technically accurate reply can still mishandle an upset customer. If you run a business, you know that a tidy report can leave out the problem everyone is quietly working around.

Those observations are useful. The next step is to make them explicit enough to guide your use of AI. Instead of asking only for an output, describe the purpose, audience, constraints and checks that make the output acceptable.

sections.heading: Practise three decisions
paragraphs: First, frame the problem. Write what the person actually needs before choosing a tool. Second, verify the result. Decide which facts need a source, which calculations need a check and which assumptions need a conversation. Third, own the action. Know who can approve it and how to correct it if it causes a problem.

Try this with an ordinary email. Ask AI for a draft, then explain why you kept one sentence and changed another. If you cannot explain your edits, you may be accepting style as a substitute for judgement. The exercise is simple, but it makes your contribution visible.

sections.heading: Build evidence of your value
paragraphs: Choose a recurring task in your field. Document how you completed it before, how you used AI and what still required your knowledge. Keep the corrections and the limitations. You are building a practical record of your thinking, not a collection of impressive prompts.

My work in AI adoption and education through ECHUKU is shaped by this concern. I want people to gain capability, not become dependent on answers they cannot evaluate. Problem-solving skills and judgement remain central to that aim.

sections.heading: Take a smaller, stronger next step
paragraphs: You do not have to abandon your profession because AI arrived. Start by finding the intersection between your existing knowledge and one useful application. Learn enough about the tool to recognise where it fails. Then show that you can use it responsibly on a real task.

That is why I created an AI Career Guide. Use it to explore possible directions, then test one against your interests and experience. A guide can help you choose a path; your practice and evidence make that path yours.

takeaway: Choose one task this week and document the three decisions only you could responsibly make: framing, verification and approval.
